job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's a section-by-section read of the text as you pasted it. I've grouped items by section so staff can map them onto the markup, but each is numbered independently. (I can't check this against the official PDF, so if the manager's amendment changed any wording, flag it and I'll re-read.)

## Sec. 2(1) — Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, so an operator can run several vessels each recovering 9,999 tons and never trigger the prohibition. There is no aggregation across a fleet, an operator, a contract area, or affiliated companies.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year."** "Year" is undefined (calendar year? license year? any rolling 12 months?), which lets an operator straddle a year boundary: e.g., 9,000 tons in December and 9,000 in January, 18,000 tons in two months without a violation under a calendar-year reading.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery."** The operative verb is never defined. In a typical system a seabed collector lifts nodules to a production vessel, which transships to a bulk carrier; it is unclear which vessel "recovers," and whether lifting, storing, transporting, or landing counts. Combined with item 1, this invites arguments that no single vessel recovered anything over the threshold.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "metric tons."** Wet versus dry weight is unspecified. Nodules lose a large share of their mass on drying, so an operator can report dry tonnage and recover far more wet material.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "at depths greater than 200 meters."** It is ambiguous whether this refers to water depth over the seabed or depth into the seabed. It also doesn't say which seabed (U.S. outer continental shelf, foreign EEZs, the Area beyond national jurisdiction), so the geographic reach of the prohibition depends entirely on the jurisdictional phrases in Sec. 3(a).

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources."** "Mineral resources" is undefined. Operators targeting seafloor massive sulfides or cobalt-rich crusts could argue they are outside the term, and nothing addresses sediment, brines, or biological material taken incidentally.

7. **Sec. 2(1) generally — the label "commercial" does no work.** The defined term says "commercial," but the definition turns only on tonnage, not on purpose or sale. A small-scale sale-for-profit operation under 10,000 tons is lawful, while a large government or academic sampling program over 10,000 tons is a crime, which is probably the reverse of what drafters intended and gives defendants a textual argument that commercial intent is an unstated element.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary."** The term is never defined. The bill mentions NOAA (Commerce) in Sec. 4 and the Secretary of State in Sec. 6, so no one can tell which official holds the catch-all authority. As drafted, this subparagraph may be unusable.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — crime by agency determination.** Because Sec. 5(b) makes violations of Sec. 3 a felony punishable by up to 10 years, this lets an executive official expand the scope of a criminal statute by finding "comparable risks," with no procedure (rulemaking, notice, publication, judicial review) specified. Expect vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges, and expect the "comparable" standard itself to be litigated.

10. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — no standard or process for the determination.** "Comparable to" is not benchmarked (comparable in area disturbed? sediment plume? species affected?), and there is no requirement that the determination be made by rule, be published, or apply only prospectively. A determination issued after an activity began could be challenged as retroactive.

## Sec. 2(2) — Definition of "U.S. person"

11. **Sec. 2(2) — foreign subsidiaries are outside the definition.** A U.S. parent can form a subsidiary in the Marshall Islands, Bermuda, Nauru, Tonga, or elsewhere and have it conduct the mining. Nothing attributes the subsidiary's conduct to the parent, and nothing covers entities "owned or controlled by" U.S. persons, which is the standard formulation in sanctions and export-control statutes. This is the single largest gap for "companies keep going."

12. **Sec. 2(2) — "corporation organized under the laws of a State."** LLCs, limited partnerships, trusts, and joint ventures are not "corporations" and are arguably excluded. "State" is undefined, so entities organized under federal law or in D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, or other territories may also be excluded.

13. **Sec. 2(2) — individuals.** Only "citizens" are covered; lawful permanent residents and other U.S. residents are not, unless they happen to be physically "in the United States" under Sec. 3(a) at the time of the conduct.

## Sec. 2(3) — Definition of "covered vessel"

14. **Sec. 2(3) — "more than 5,000 gross tons."** The registry excludes smaller vessels, so an operator using a vessel under 5,000 GT (or splitting the system into multiple small vessels, see item 1) is never registered and never reports.

15. **Sec. 2(3) — "equipped for the recovery."** A barge or support ship that carries a detachable collector or ROV, or a vessel that is "equipped" only while on station, can argue it is not a covered vessel. The term also isn't tied to the 200-meter depth or to any jurisdictional nexus, so on its face it reaches every mining-capable vessel in the world.

## Sec. 3 — Prohibition and exceptions

16. **Sec. 3(a) — "engage in."** Undefined. It is unclear whether financing, insuring, chartering a vessel, supplying equipment, providing crew, processing or refining nodules, or importing mined material counts as "engaging." Without an aiding-and-abetting, facilitation, or import provision, U.S. companies can finance and buy from foreign operators and U.S. ports can service their vessels.

17. **Sec. 3(a) — "any person in the United States."** "Person" is undefined (it does not pick up the "U.S. person" definition), and "in the United States" is undefined; it is unclear whether it includes the EEZ, the outer continental shelf, territories, or U.S.-flagged vessels. Since the activity itself happens far offshore, this prong may reach almost no actual mining.

18. **Sec. 3(a) — no interaction with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act.** The 1980 Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) authorizes NOAA to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, and the bill neither repeals nor amends it. Two statutes would then point in opposite directions, and a permit holder would argue the more specific, pre-existing authorization controls or that the later Act must be read narrowly to avoid conflict.

19. **Sec. 3(b) — grandfathers "exploration" licenses, not commercial permits.** An exploration license does not ordinarily authorize commercial recovery, so the exception either (a) means nothing, or (b) is read to allow full commercial mining by anyone holding any pre-enactment exploration license. Courts will have to pick, and the broad reading swallows the prohibition for every incumbent. Conversely, a commercial recovery permit issued before enactment is, oddly, not grandfathered.

20. **Sec. 3(b) — issuer unspecified.** "An exploration license" could be one issued by NOAA, by the International Seabed Authority (which calls them contracts, not licenses), or by any foreign government. Any state willing to issue paper before enactment can create a permanent exemption.

21. **Sec. 3(b) — rush window and no limits.** Because the cutoff is the date of enactment (not introduction or committee report), there is an incentive to obtain licenses during the legislative process. The exception has no volume cap, no expiration, no condition that the license remain valid, and no bar on transferring the license or the licensee to new owners.

22. **Sec. 3(c) — the environmental-assessment exception is purpose-based with no limits.** Any recovery can be characterized as a "collector test" or "impact study." There is no tonnage cap, no approving agency, no requirement that results be reported or that recovered material not be sold. As drafted, this is a complete workaround.

## Sec. 4 — Registry

23. **Sec. 4 — no penalty for noncompliance.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failure to register, failure to report, and false certification carry no consequence under this Act (the general false-statements statute, 18 U.S.C. 1001, might apply to a false certification, but the bill doesn't say so).

24. **Sec. 4 — no deadline, nexus, or rulemaking authority.** There is no date by which registration is due, no statement of which operators are subject (a foreign operator of a foreign-flagged vessel is literally covered but practically unreachable), no definition of "operator," and no grant of authority to NOAA to issue regulations or forms.

25. **Sec. 4(b) — reports don't have to include tonnage.** A report "describing the recovery activities" need not state quantities recovered, so NOAA has no mandated data to test the 10,000-ton threshold. There is also no inspection, audit, recordkeeping, or vessel-monitoring authority, and reports are self-certified only.

## Sec. 5 — Penalties

26. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8 — penalty applies before the prohibition exists.** Civil penalties attach to "any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment," but under Sec. 8 the Act (including Sec. 3) does not take effect until 180 days later. Conduct in that window cannot "violate" a prohibition not yet in force, and any attempt to penalize it invites a retroactivity challenge.

27. **Sec. 5(a) — daily penalty for an annual offense.** The violation is defined by tonnage "per year," but the penalty is "for each day on which the violation occurs." It is unclear whether the violation "occurs" only on the day the threshold is crossed, on every day thereafter, or on every day of the year retroactively; this will be litigated in the first enforcement action.

28. **Sec. 5 — no enforcing agency or procedure.** The bill never says who assesses civil penalties (NOAA? Justice? Coast Guard?), whether assessment is administrative or judicial, what the statute of limitations is, or how penalties are collected. There is no injunctive relief, no authority to seize or forfeit vessels or recovered minerals, no in rem jurisdiction, and no citizen-suit provision.

29. **Sec. 5(a) — no floor and no inflation adjustment.** "Not more than $1,000,000" allows nominal penalties, and without reference to the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act the cap erodes over the 10-year life of the Act.

30. **Sec. 5(b) — criminal liability tied to item 9.** Because the offense incorporates Sec. 2(1)(B), a felony conviction could rest on an undefined official's "comparable risk" finding. There is also no provision for corporate-officer liability or for penalties against the vessel.

## Sec. 6 — International agreement

31. **Sec. 6 — unenforceable and ambiguous timing.** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude anything, and the 18-month clause can be read to modify either "seek" or "negotiate," so it is unclear what must happen by then. There is no report-to-Congress requirement, and the section doesn't address the International Seabed Authority or the fact that the United States is not a party to UNCLOS.

## Sec. 7 — Duration

32. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) — direct conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress finds mining can be done safely; subsection (b) says the entire Act expires after 10 years regardless. The sunset controls, so the "until Congress finds" language is illusory and the title "Prohibition" is in practice a 10-year moratorium.

33. **Sec. 7(a) — the National Academies report is unfunded and unrequested.** Nothing directs or funds the Academies to produce a report, sets a deadline, or defines "serious harm." And because a joint resolution is itself a law, the subsection adds nothing; Congress can always repeal the Act by statute.

34. **Sec. 7(b) — sunset of the whole Act, no savings clause.** On the sunset date the definitions, registry, and penalty provisions all vanish. Without a savings clause, defendants will argue that pending enforcement actions and penalties for pre-sunset violations lapse with the statute.

## Sec. 8 and cross-cutting drafting issues

35. **Sec. 8 — the 180-day delay interacts badly with Sec. 3(b).** Licenses issued between enactment and the effective date are not grandfathered, yet mining under them isn't prohibited either during those 180 days, producing a six-month period of legal limbo.

36. **No severability clause.** If Sec. 2(1)(B) or another provision is struck down (see items 8–10), a court could hold the whole Act falls with it.

37. **No rulemaking authority anywhere in the Act.** No agency is authorized to define terms, set reporting formats, or fill the gaps noted above, which both weakens enforcement and makes any agency attempt to do so vulnerable to challenge.

38. **Missing definitions.** "Person," "Secretary," "recovery," "year," "operator," "vessel," "State," "seabed," "mineral resources," and "serious harm" are all undefined; several are outcome-determinative.

39. **No import or supply-chain provision.** Nothing prohibits importing, processing, or selling nodules or metals recovered by foreign operators, so the U.S. market remains fully open to deep-seabed minerals and U.S. firms can participate as buyers, financiers, and refiners.

If it's useful for the story, the items most likely to come up at markup are probably 1 (fleet splitting), 11 (foreign subsidiaries), 19–22 (the two exceptions), 26 and 32 (internal conflicts), and 8–9 (the undefined "Secretary" and the delegated criminal definition), since those are the ones opposing offices and committee counsel are most likely to have spotted too.
